title: Lost on the Reef
summary: Two brothers drift away from their boat while snorkeling near a reef and must use a current and a landmark to swim safely back to shore.
poll: Children should never be allowed to snorkel near a reef without an adult swimming right beside them.

versions.title: Lost on the Reef
versions.text:
Faisal and Yousef go to the sea. Uncle Khalid takes them. He has a boat.

They see a reef. It has fish. The fish are yellow and blue.

"Stay near me," says Uncle Khalid. "If you get lost, find the red flag. It is on the shore."

The boys put on masks. They put on fins. They jump in the water.

They swim after the fish. They do not look back. The boat is far now.

The water pulls them. This is a current. Yousef feels scared.

"Do not panic," says Faisal. "Find the flag." They see it far away.

They swim to the side. Not straight. This is the right way. They swim and swim.

At last, they reach the shore! Uncle Khalid runs to them. He is so glad. The boys are safe.

versions.title: Lost on the Reef
versions.text:
Faisal and his brother Yousef love the sea. One morning, their uncle Khalid takes them out on his small boat to see a reef.

"Stay close to the boat," Uncle Khalid warns. "If you get lost, look for the red flag near the shore. That flag is your landmark."

The boys put on masks and fins. They jump into the warm water. They see fish in bright colors. Some fish are yellow. Some are blue.

The boys swim after the fish. They do not look back. The boat drifts far behind them. A current is pulling them, but they do not feel it yet.

Yousef looks around. He cannot see the boat. He feels scared. "Don't panic," Faisal tells him. "Let's find the flag." They look at the shore and spot it, far away.

The boys swim to the side, not straight. This helps them move with the current. They swim and swim. Their arms feel tired.

At last, their feet touch the sand. Uncle Khalid runs down the beach. "I was so worried!" he says, and hugs them tight. The boys are safe.

versions.title: Lost on the Reef
versions.text:
Faisal and his younger brother Yousef love the sea. One calm morning, their uncle Khalid takes them out on his small boat to see a coral reef near the shore.

Before they swim, Uncle Khalid gives them a rule. "Stay close to the boat," he says. "If we get separated, look for the red flag on the beach. That flag is your landmark home."

The boys put on their masks and fins and slip into the warm water. Right away, they see fish in bright colors — yellow, blue, and orange — swimming near the rocks.

The boys swim after the fish and forget to look back. Slowly, the boat drifts farther away. A current, a steady pull of water, is quietly carrying them along, though neither boy notices at first.

When Yousef looks up, the boat is gone. Fear rises in his chest. "Don't panic," Faisal says, trying to sound brave. "Let's find the flag." They look at the shore and spot a tiny red dot.

Instead of swimming straight against the current, the boys swim to the side, cutting across it toward the flag. This way, the water helps push them home.

They swim on, resting for a moment when their arms grow heavy. Slowly, the shore grows closer. At last, their feet touch solid sand. Uncle Khalid runs down the beach and pulls them into a hug. "I was so worried!" he says. Tired but safe, the boys will not forget that little red flag.

Faisal and his younger brother Yousef loved every trip to the sea, but this trip would be one they never forgot. One calm morning, their uncle Khalid took them out on his small boat to see a coral reef just off the coast.

Before the boys got in the water, Uncle Khalid gave them an important rule. "Stay close to the boat," he said. "If we get separated, look back for the red flag on the beach. That flag is your landmark — it will always point you home."

The boys pulled on their masks and fins and slipped into the warm water. Almost at once, they spotted fish in bright colors, yellow, blue, and orange, darting near the rocks and coral.

Excited, the boys swam after the fish without checking behind them. Slowly, the small boat drifted farther and farther away. A current, a steady pull of water under the surface, was quietly carrying the boys along, though neither one noticed at first.

When Yousef finally looked up, the boat was gone. Fear rose in his chest. "Don't panic," Faisal said, trying to sound braver than he felt. "Let's find the flag first." They searched the shore and spotted it, a tiny red dot far away.

Instead of swimming straight against the pull, the boys remembered their uncle's rule and swam sideways, cutting across the current toward the flag. This way, the water helped carry them toward shore.

They swam on, resting for a moment whenever their arms grew too tired. Slowly, the shoreline grew closer. At last, their feet touched solid sand. Uncle Khalid came running down the beach and pulled the boys into a tight hug. "I was so worried about you two!" he said. Tired but safe, the boys would never forget that little red flag.

versions.title: Lost on the Reef
versions.text:
Every summer, Faisal and his younger brother Yousef counted down the days until their uncle Khalid took them out on his fishing boat. This trip would teach them something they never forgot.

Before the boat left the dock, Uncle Khalid gave the boys a serious talk. "The sea is beautiful, but it is also powerful," he said. "A current is water that moves steadily in one direction, almost like a river inside the sea. If you ever feel one pulling you, do not swim straight against it, or you will exhaust yourself. Swim sideways, across it, toward the shore. And always remember your landmark: that red flag on the beach will show you the way home."

Once they reached the reef, the boys pulled on their masks and fins and slipped into the warm water. Beneath the surface, a world of color opened up. Parrotfish nibbled at the coral, and tiny orange clownfish darted between the swaying plants.

Excited by the sight, the boys swam after the fish, drifting farther from the boat with every minute. Neither of them noticed that the current was quietly pulling them sideways.

When Yousef lifted his head, his stomach dropped. The boat was nowhere in sight. "Don't panic," Faisal said, though his heart was pounding. "Remember what Uncle Khalid told us. Find the flag." They squinted at the shore and spotted it, a tiny red speck far away.

Instead of swimming straight against the current, the boys angled their strokes sideways, cutting across it toward the flag, just as their uncle had taught them. Slowly, the current began to help them instead of fight them.

They swam on, pausing now and then to catch their breath. Bit by bit, the shore grew closer.

At last, tired but determined, their feet touched the sandy bottom. Just then, Uncle Khalid came running down the beach, his face full of worry and relief. He pulled both boys into a hug. "Thank goodness you remembered the flag," he said. The boys, tired but safe, knew they would not forget that lesson.

versions.title: Lost on the Reef
versions.text:
Every summer, Faisal and his younger brother Yousef counted down the days until their uncle Khalid invited them snorkeling along the reefs of the Red Sea. This particular excursion, however, would teach the brothers an unforgettable lesson about respecting the power of the sea.

Before the boat had even left the dock, Uncle Khalid sat the boys down for a serious conversation, his tone calm but deliberate. "The sea is beautiful, but it is also powerful," he explained, gesturing toward the glittering water. "A current is a steady movement of water in one direction, almost like a hidden river flowing within the sea itself. If you ever feel one pulling you, never swim directly against it, since that will only lead to exhaustion. Instead, swim diagonally, cutting across the current toward the shore. And always keep your landmark in sight — that tall red flag on the beach will help you navigate home, no matter how disoriented you might feel."

Once they reached the reef, the boys pulled on their masks and fins and slipped into the warm, translucent water. Beneath the surface, an entire world of color unfolded: striped parrotfish grazed on coral, tiny clownfish darted among swaying anemones, and a sea turtle glided serenely past, entirely unbothered by the two curious boys.

Captivated by the scene, the boys swam after the fish, drifting steadily farther from the boat. Neither noticed that an invisible current beneath the surface was carrying them sideways.

When Yousef lifted his head to check on the boat, his stomach lurched; it was nowhere to be seen, and for a terrifying moment he felt completely disoriented. "Don't panic," Faisal said, struggling to maintain his own composure even as his heart pounded against his ribs. "Remember what Uncle Khalid told us. Find the flag." Squinting toward the shore, they located it, a tiny red speck nearly swallowed by the glare of sunlight.

Rather than exhausting themselves fighting the current head-on, the boys angled their strokes sideways, cutting diagonally toward the flag, exactly as their uncle had instructed. Gradually, the current began working with them instead of against them.

They swam on, pausing occasionally to float on their backs, recover from the exertion, and call out encouragement to one another. Stroke by stroke, the shoreline grew closer, and the knot of fear in Yousef's chest slowly began to loosen.

At last, utterly exhausted but triumphant, their feet touched the sandy bottom. At that very moment, Uncle Khalid came sprinting down the beach, his expression a mixture of panic and relief; he pulled both boys into a fierce embrace, momentarily unable to speak.

Once he had regained his composure, Uncle Khalid knelt beside them and explained that what had swept them sideways was a longshore current, a common force along reefs that moves water parallel to the shoreline. "Thank goodness you kept your composure instead of succumbing to panic," he said. That evening, the boys recounted the experience to their parents, proud that they had stayed calm despite their fatigue and fear.

Before the boat had even left the dock, Uncle Khalid sat the boys down for a serious conversation. The sea, he explained, was beautiful but undeniably powerful, since a current was simply a steady movement of water in one direction, functioning almost like a hidden river flowing within the ocean itself. Currents often formed near reefs because water funneled through narrow gaps in the coral, gaining considerable speed as it squeezed through those tight channels; oceanographers who study coastal waters note that such currents can shift in strength within minutes, which is precisely why experienced swimmers treat the sea with caution rather than overconfidence. Should either boy ever feel a current pulling him along, Uncle Khalid warned, he must never attempt to swim directly against it, since doing so would only lead to rapid exhaustion; instead, he should swim diagonally, cutting across the current toward shore, always keeping the tall red flag on the beach in sight as a landmark capable of guiding him home regardless of how disoriented he might feel.

Once they reached the reef, the boys pulled on their masks and fins and slipped into the warm, translucent water, where an entire world of color unfolded beneath them, striped parrotfish grazing methodically on coral while tiny clownfish darted among swaying anemones, and a sea turtle glided serenely past, entirely unbothered by its two young observers. Captivated by the scene, the boys swam after the fish, drifting steadily farther from the boat, their attention entirely consumed by the vivid underwater world, and neither noticed that an invisible current beneath the surface was carrying them sideways, propelled by the very funneling effect their uncle had described only an hour earlier.

When Yousef lifted his head to check the boat's position, his stomach lurched violently: it was nowhere to be seen, and for a genuinely terrifying moment he felt completely disoriented, unable to judge which direction led back to safety. "Don't panic," Faisal said, struggling visibly to maintain his own composure even as his heart pounded against his ribs. "Remember what Uncle Khalid told us. Find the flag first." Squinting toward the shore, they located it, a tiny red speck nearly swallowed by the blinding glare of sunlight reflecting off the water.

Rather than exhausting themselves fighting the current's pull head-on, the boys angled their strokes sideways, cutting diagonally toward the flag exactly as their uncle had instructed, and gradually the current began working in their favor rather than against them, carrying them steadily toward shore with every deliberate stroke. They swam on, pausing occasionally to float on their backs, recover from the mounting exertion, and call out encouragement to one another whenever their resolve began to waver, and stroke by stroke the shoreline grew closer, loosening the knot of fear and fatigue lodged in Yousef's chest.

At last, utterly exhausted but triumphant, their feet touched the sandy bottom. At that very moment, Uncle Khalid came sprinting down the beach, his expression a volatile mixture of panic and relief, and he pulled both boys into a fierce embrace, momentarily unable to speak through his emotion. Once he had regained his composure, he knelt beside them in the sand and explained that what had swept them sideways was known as a longshore current, a common force along reefs that moves water parallel to the shoreline rather than directly out to sea. The following week, determined that his nephews would learn to navigate the sea with genuine confidence rather than relying on luck, Uncle Khalid enrolled both boys in a formal water-safety course.

Years later, whenever Faisal and Yousef returned to that stretch of coastline, they would glance instinctively toward the red flag before swimming near the reef, a habit born from the afternoon they had drifted dangerously far from safety and found their way back through calm thinking rather than panic. In many ways, the ordeal became more than a frightening afternoon in the water; it became a quiet lesson in resilience, the kind that resurfaces decades later in subtler moments of difficulty, reminding them that genuine courage rarely looks dramatic from the outside but more often resembles two tired, frightened boys choosing, again and again, to breathe steadily, think clearly, and keep swimming toward home.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says children should never be allowed to snorkel near a reef without an adult swimming right beside them. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the current, the landmark, and how the boys reacted.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I partly disagree that children should never snorkel near a reef without an adult right beside them. The story shows that Faisal and Yousef survived because Uncle Khalid had already taught them what to do before the swim, not because an adult was swimming between them at every moment. They used his advice about swimming diagonally across the current and watching for the landmark to get safely to shore. Someone might argue that an adult nearby could have prevented the danger entirely, which is true, but the story also shows that clear preparation and calm thinking can be just as important as constant supervision.
